title: Chords in a Key
goal: Know the seven chords of a major key by number, play the progressions a great many songs are made of with small shapes, and move any of them to another key.
assumes: You can play major and minor triads in three shapes on the top strings and change between C, A minor, F and G with the nearest shapes at 90 BPM: the first two Levels of Triads. The shapes on the D, G and B strings are shown as they come. No other theory is assumed. The minutes listed are one pass through the material; the progressions are worth coming back to in every key you play in.

skills: Major and minor triads on the top strings
Eighth notes with a click at 80 BPM

orderRationale: All seven chords of the key first, built in order from the scale, because the pattern of major and minor is the thing to learn and it is the same in every key. Numbers come next and letters go into the background: a progression is a set of numbers, and a key is where you put them. The three major chords come before the three minor ones because most songs can be played with them alone. Named progressions follow, one at a time. One, four and five move to other keys as soon as they have numbers; the longer progressions move later, once the numbers are familiar, so that changing key is moving a known thing. The minor key is late because it is the same seven chords counted from a different one. Longer forms follow: twelve bars, a verse and a chorus, then sixteen bars with a bridge. Each idea is given a second and a third key before the next arrives (G and A in full, E minor after A minor), because a number only becomes a number once it has stood for several different chords. Chords from outside the key wait until the key itself is secure, and the seventh chords come last: they are the same seven chords with one more note each, and they hand the player on to Arpeggios over Changes.
gradingLimits: Every graded Exercise is played one note at a time: after the take, the app checks that you played the written notes, counts them and times them. It cannot tell which string a pitch came from, so a right note in the wrong place passes, and it cannot hear whether you held each shape down like a chord. Strummed chords are not graded anywhere in this Path. It cannot hear you say a chord's number either: that part is yours. The band Exercises have only been tried on computer-made guitar sound, so direct input or headphones are the honest way to play them. Choosing your own chords and shapes is 'your turn', self-checked and labelled 'not checked yet'.

steps.title: A chord on every note
steps.goal: Build a triad on each note of the C major scale, play all seven in order, and say which are major and which are minor.
steps.why: A key is a scale, and the chords of a key are what you get by building a triad on each of its notes using only notes of that scale. Do that in C and seven chords come out: C, D minor, E minor, F, G, A minor and one odd one on B. You did not choose which are major and which are minor: the scale did. The pattern is the same in every major key, which is why learning it once is enough.
howTo: The pattern: major, minor, minor, major, major, minor, and the seventh is called diminished. Say it until it is automatic.
Diminished is a minor triad with its fifth lowered one fret too: B minor would be B, D, F sharp, and B diminished is B, D, F. It sounds unsettled, and songs use it rarely. Know it exists and move on.
In the first two Exercises the root is the lowest note of every shape, so you can follow it up the scale. The third uses the nearest shapes, where the root is often not the lowest note.
To build them yourself: start on any note of the scale, skip the next, take the one after, skip, take. C, E, G. D, F, A. E, G, B. And so on.
steps.payoff: You can name the seven chords of C major and play them in order.

steps.title: Chords have numbers
steps.goal: Call the chords of a key by number, play the first, fourth and fifth in an eight-bar form, and play the same numbers in other keys.
steps.why: Musicians number the chords of a key from one to seven, the same way you numbered the notes of the scale. C is one, F is four, G is five. The reason is practical: a song is the same song in any key, and its numbers do not change when its letters do. 'One, four, five' is a great many songs. Written down, the numbers are Roman numerals: I, IV, V. Minor chords are usually written small: ii, iii, vi.
howTo: In C: one is C, four is F, five is G. They are the three major chords of the key.
Five wants to go home to one. Play G and then C and listen to it arrive.
In any other key, find one, and four and five are in the same places around it in the shapes you know.
steps.payoff: You hear 'one, four, five' and your hand knows three shapes, in whatever key is called.

steps.title: Two, three and six
steps.goal: Pair each major chord of the key with the minor chord two scale notes below it, which shares two of its notes, and play one, six, two, five.
steps.why: The three minor chords of the key are not strangers. Each one is a major chord with one note moved: C and A minor share C and E, F and D minor share F and A, G and E minor share G and B. That is why a song can swap one for the other and sound like a darker version of the same song. Six, two and three are the numbers of A minor, D minor and E minor in the key of C.
howTo: C to A minor: G moves up to A, on the top string, fret 3 to fret 5.
F to D minor: C moves up to D, on the G string, fret 5 to fret 7.
G to E minor: D moves up to E, on the B string, fret 3 to fret 5.
steps.payoff: Six chords that feel like three pairs, and one of the most used four-chord turns in older songs: one, six, two, five.

steps.title: Three progressions worth knowing by name
steps.goal: Play two, five, one; six, four, one, five; and one, three, four, five, each with the nearest shapes.
steps.why: A progression is a short run of chord numbers that turns up in song after song. Learn a handful as numbers and you can follow most songs by ear, because you are listening for a few known shapes instead of every chord from scratch. These three, with the ones you have, cover a very large part of popular music.
howTo: Two, five, one (D minor, G, C) is a very strong way home. Jazz uses it constantly, and pop uses it at the ends of lines.

Six, four, one, five (A minor, F, C, G) is the song from Triads, C, G, A minor, F, which is one, five, six, four, started from its third chord. Starting on the minor chord makes the same four sound darker.

One, three, four, five (C, E minor, F, G) climbs through the scale: its roots are notes one, three, four and five. In these shapes the root is not always the lowest note, so listen for the band's bass rising.
steps.payoff: Three more progressions you can name when you hear them.

steps.title: The same numbers, other keys
steps.goal: Play the seven chords of D major, and move one, six, two, five and two, five, one to keys that change from day to day.
steps.why: This is where the numbers pay for themselves. To play a song in a new key you do not learn new chords: you move the whole picture up or down the neck until one sits on the new key's note, and every number comes with it. The pattern of major and minor comes too, because it belongs to the numbers and not to the letters.
howTo: D is two frets above C, so every chord of D major is two frets above the matching chord of C major: D, E minor, F sharp minor, G, A, B minor, C sharp diminished.
Before you play in a new key, say its one, four and five out loud. To name them, move the C names up by the same number of frets: two frets above C is D, two above F is G, two above G is A.
The shapes and the fingers do not change at all. Only the fret does.
steps.payoff: A progression is something you can play in any key you are asked for.

steps.goal: Play the seven chords of G major, its one, four and five in an eight-bar form, and its one, six, two, five.

steps.title: One, five, six, four
steps.goal: Play one, five, six, four in G and in A, the same four chords in the order one, six, four, five, and one, five, six, four in keys that change.
steps.why: If one progression had to stand for the popular music of the last sixty years, it would be one, five, six, four. In C it is C, G, A minor, F: the eight-bar song in Triads. Start the same loop on its third chord and it is six, four, one, five, which you have played too. Put the chords in the order one, six, four, five and you have the sound of the nineteen-fifties. steps.title: The minor key
steps.goal: Play the main chords of A minor, and hear why its fifth chord is so often made major.
steps.why: A minor uses exactly the same seven notes as C major, and so the same seven chords. What changes is which one feels like home: A minor instead of C. Count from there and A minor is one, D minor is four, E minor is five, and F and G are six and seven, C is three and B diminished is two. The numbers start again from the new home: F was four in C major and is six in A minor, the same chord counted from a different one. A minor is called the relative minor of C major. One thing is new. Minor-key songs very often turn the fifth chord, E minor, into E major, because its G sharp pulls back to A much harder. It is the one note from outside the scale that you will meet all the time.

Six and seven, F and G, are the two major chords just below home. A minor, F, G, A minor is the sound of a great deal of rock.
E major is E, G sharp, B. E minor is 4, 5, 3 and E major is 4, 5, 4: only the top string changes, G to G sharp, one fret below A.
steps.payoff: You can play the main chords of a minor key, and you know why its fifth chord is so often major.

steps.title: Chords from outside the key
steps.goal: Play the three chords songs most often take from outside the key, the flat seven, the major two and the minor four, and hear the one note each of them changes.
steps.why: The seven chords of a key are the ones a song can use without surprising anyone. Songs surprise people on purpose. Three outside chords turn up again and again, and each is made by changing a single note of the scale. Lower the seventh note and a major chord appears a whole step below home: in C, B flat. Raise the fourth note and the two chord turns major: D instead of D minor. Lower the sixth note and the four chord turns minor: F minor instead of F. You do not need the theory to use them. You need to know where they sit beside the chords you have.
howTo: The flat seven is the one chord moved two frets down, same shape. C is 5, 5, 3, so B flat is 3, 3, 1.
The major two: D minor is 7, 6, 5 and D major is 7, 7, 5. The new note is F sharp, one fret under G, which is why it leans toward the five chord.
The minor four: F is 5, 6, 5 and F minor is 5, 6, 4. The new note is A flat, one fret above G, and it falls to the G of a C chord.
steps.payoff: Three chords that are not in the key and belong in its songs, each found from a chord you know.

exercises.title: One, flat seven, four, one
exercises.purpose: C, B flat, F, C. B flat is the C shape two frets lower, and F sits right under it.
howTo: Straight eighths, 60 BPM up to a pass at 90. One bar on each chord.
On the G, B and top strings: C is 5, 5, 3. B flat is 3, 3, 1. F is 2, 1, 1. C again.
B flat is not one of the seven chords of C: its root is one fret lower than the scale's seventh note. Listen for how it loosens the key.
exercises.coachLine: Band on. Right notes and time after the take.

C is 5, 5, 3. D major is 7, 7, 5: the C shape two frets up. G is 7, 8, 7. C is 9, 8, 8.
The F sharp in the D chord, B string fret 7, moves up one fret to G in the next bar. That half step is why this D wants to go to G.

steps.title: Four notes: the seventh chords of the key
steps.goal: Add the seventh to each chord of the key, play the four kinds of chord that come out, and play all seven in order with the root on the A string and then on the low E string.
steps.why: A triad is every other note of the scale, three of them: one, three, five. Take one more, the seventh, and you have a seventh chord. Do that on each note of the C scale, using only the scale's notes, and four kinds come out. C and F become major seven chords, soft and open. D minor, E minor and A minor become minor seven, smoother than plain minor. G becomes G seven, the one restless chord of the key, which is why five leads home. B becomes B half-diminished: the diminished triad with a seventh on top. Once again you did not choose. The scale did. These are four-string shapes with the root on the A string or the low E string, and they are the chords of soul, bossa nova, jazz and a good deal of pop.
howTo: The pattern, to say until it is automatic: major seven, minor seven, minor seven, major seven, seven, minor seven, half-diminished.
Root on the A string, then the D, G and B strings. C major seven: 3, 5, 4, 5. D minor seven: 5, 7, 5, 6. G seven: 10, 12, 10, 12. B half-diminished, written Bm7b5: 2, 3, 2, 3.
Root on the low E string, leave out the A string, then the D, G and B strings. G seven: 3, 3, 4, 3. A minor seven: the first finger across fret 5. C major seven: 8, 9, 9, 8.
Each bar goes up through the four strings, back down, and plays the second-lowest string of the shape once more.
steps.payoff: The four kinds of seventh chord a key contains, and all seven of them in order.

exercises.title: C and F become major seven
exercises.purpose: C, then C major seven; F, then F major seven. In each pair one note moves: the root on the G string drops one fret and becomes the seventh.
howTo: Straight eighths, 50 BPM up to a pass at 80. One bar on each chord: up through the four strings, back down, and the D string once more.

C: A string 3, then the third finger laid flat across fret 5 on the D, G and B strings. C major seven: A string 3, D string 5, G string 4, B string 5. The third finger stays on the D string, the second finger takes the G string and the fourth takes the B string.
F and F major seven are the same two shapes five frets higher: A string 8 with fret 10 above it, and then 8, 10, 9, 10.
exercises.coachLine: Right notes and even eighths after the take. Listen to what the one fret does.

exercises.title: D minor and E minor become minor seven
exercises.purpose: D minor, then D minor seven; E minor, then E minor seven. In each pair the root on the G string drops two frets and becomes the seventh.
howTo: Straight eighths, 50 BPM up to a pass at 80. One bar on each chord: up through the four strings, back down, and the D string once more.
D minor: A string 5, D string 7, G string 7, B string 6. D minor seven: 5, 7, 5, 6. Lift the fourth finger, and let the first finger lie flat so it holds the G string at fret 5 as well.
E minor and E minor seven are the same two shapes two frets higher: 7, 9, 9, 8 and then 7, 9, 7, 8.
exercises.coachLine: Right notes and even eighths after the take.

exercises.title: G seven and B half-diminished
exercises.purpose: The two kinds that appear once each in a key. G, then G seven: the chord that pulls home. B diminished, then B half-diminished.
howTo: Straight eighths, 50 BPM up to a pass at 80. One bar on each chord: up through the four strings, back down, and the D string once more.

G: A string 10, then the third finger across fret 12 on the D, G and B strings. G seven: 10, 12, 10, 12. The first finger lies flat and takes the G string at fret 10, and the fourth finger takes the B string.
B diminished: A string 2, D string 3, G string 4, B string 3. B half-diminished: 2, 3, 2, 3. Lift the fourth finger and the first finger, lying flat, takes the G string at fret 2.
It is a long move from fret 10 down to fret 2 between bars 2 and 3. Look at the second fret before you leave.
exercises.coachLine: Right notes and even eighths after the take.

exercises.title: All seven, with their sevenths
exercises.purpose: Eight bars: a seventh chord on every note of the scale. The first four have their root on the A string, the last four on the low E string, at the same four frets.
howTo: Straight eighths, 60 BPM up to a pass at 85. One bar on each chord.
Bars 1 to 4, root on the A string at frets 3, 5, 7 and 8: C major seven is 3, 5, 4, 5. D minor seven is 5, 7, 5, 6. E minor seven is 7, 9, 7, 8. F major seven is 8, 10, 9, 10.

Bars 5 to 8, root on the low E string at frets 3, 5, 7 and 8, with the A string left out: G seven is 3, 3, 4, 3. A minor seven is 5, 5, 5, 5. B half-diminished is 7, 7, 7, 6. C major seven is 8, 9, 9, 8.
The roots spell the scale: C, D, E, F on the A string, then G, A, B, C on the low E string.
exercises.coachLine: Eight bars with the band. Right notes and time after the take.

steps.title: Sevenths in the progressions you know
steps.goal: Play two, five, one and one, six, two, five in seventh chords, move them to other keys, and then play them as whole chords in your own rhythm.
steps.why: Nothing about a progression changes when its chords gain a seventh: two, five, one is still two, five, one. What changes is the colour, and how smoothly one chord hands over to the next, because with four notes there is nearly always one that stays. These chords, in these shapes, are the first thing a player learns when they start on jazz or bossa nova. They are also the doorway to the next Path, Arpeggios over Changes, which plays the same chords one note at a time as a melody.
howTo: Two, five, one: D minor seven with its root on the A string at fret 5, G seven with its root on the low E string at fret 3, C major seven with its root on the A string at fret 3. The roots go D, G, C.
One, six, two, five: C major seven, A minor seven with its root on the low E string at fret 5, D minor seven, G seven.
The roots swap between the two lowest strings, and the hand stays between frets 3 and 7.
steps.payoff: The two most-used progressions of jazz and soul in seventh chords, in four keys.

exercises.title: Two, five, one in sevenths

D minor seven: A string 5, D string 7, G string 5, B string 6. G seven: low E string 3, D string 3, G string 4, B string 3. C major seven: A string 3, D string 5, G string 4, B string 5.
In G seven the low E string is followed by the D string: the pick skips the A string.

levels.title: Beginner: seven chords from one scale
levels.summary: A triad on every note of the scale, the pattern of major and minor, chords called by number, one, four and five in C and in a second key, and the three minor chords as partners of the major ones.

startHereIf: You can change between C, A minor, F and G with triads at 80 BPM.
You know some chords and could not say which of them belong to 1 key.
You don't yet know what 'one, four, five' means.

warmups.title: The first four chords of a key
warmups.purpose: Chords one, two, three and four of a major key, root lowest, climbing the G string: major, minor, minor, major. A different key each time.
howTo: Straight eighths, well under your clean tempo. Say major or minor at each bar line.
warmups.coachLine: This is a warm-up. It tells you how it went, and it decides nothing.

levels.title: Intermediate: progressions, keys, and the minor key
levels.summary: Two, five, one and two more named progressions, the seven chords of D, progressions in keys that change, the keys of G and A in full, one, five, six, four in five keys, and the main chords of a minor key in A minor and in E minor.

startHereIf: You can name the 7 chords of C major and say which are minor.
You can play one, six, two, five in C with triads at 90 BPM.
You can't yet move a progression to another key without working out every chord.

warmups.title: One, six, two, five, low then high
warmups.purpose: The turn round four chords in a key you did not play yesterday: one and six low, two and five a shape higher.
howTo: Straight eighths, well under your clean tempo. Two is a first finger laid across one fret. Say the numbers at each bar line.
warmups.coachLine: This is a warm-up. It tells you how it went, and it decides nothing.

levels.title: Advanced: forms, borrowed chords, and sevenths
levels.summary: One progression in two parts of the neck, the twelve-bar form in more than one key, a verse and a chorus built from four chords, a sixteen-bar form with a bridge, three chords from outside the key, and the seventh chords of the key in the progressions you know.

startHereIf: You can play two, five, one and one, six, two, five in 3 keys.
You know the main chords of a minor key.
You lose your place in forms longer than 4 bars, or you only know each progression in 1 part of the neck.
